content:
How do we test what an AI agent produced before it touches real systems or real users?
Static checks, unit tests, and prompt evals verify syntax and isolated assertions. They miss hallucinations and alignment failures that only surface when an agent’s output meets stateful systems and unpredictable users.
Verified software for the agentic era checks whether third-party tools and libraries are safe before an agent adopts them. Proof of Human Intent verifies that a person explicitly approved a consequential action. Between those two boundaries sits the agent’s own output: code patches, database queries, multi-step tool plans, and user-facing workflows.
One way to validate that output is to run it inside an ephemeral world simulation before promoting anything to production.
What isolated checks miss When an agent changes code or plans a workflow, standard validation leaves three blind spots:
Self-confirming mocks hide real failure modes. When an agent writes both a change and its unit tests, both come from the same pass over the problem. If the agent misreads how an external API behaves on timeout, it mocks that API with the same wrong assumption. Under retries or concurrent requests, the code breaks. Hallucinations can still compile and return 200. An agent might drop a query filter, invent a fallback state, or mutate the wrong record while returning a confident summary. Single-turn evals miss interactive misalignment. An agent may follow policy in a clean prompt test and violate it during a multi-turn conversation when a user pushes back, repeats an ambiguous request, or embeds instructions inside untrusted text. How a world simulation works A world-simulation validator runs the candidate change inside a temporary environment made of two parts:
Stateful software sandboxes: Isolated clones or seeded replicas of databases, queues, identity rules, and mocked external APIs, paired with fault injection (timeouts, dropped responses, rate limits, partial failures). Simulated humans and adversaries: Automated user personas and red-team agents that send messy requests, retry impatiently, trigger race conditions, or try to extract data and override rules. The agent under test cannot own this environment. If the same agent can edit the world definition, service mocks, or invariant rules, it can shape the test around its own assumptions. Keeping the simulation harness outside the agent’s workspace turns it into an independent gate.
A validation run follows four steps:
Snapshot the starting world. Spin up a disposable environment from a known seed: schema, anonymized sample state, permission boundaries, service mocks, and fault profiles. Run the candidate output or tool plan. Apply a code patch in the sandbox, or run shadow execution for a tool-using agent by sending its proposed tool calls against cloned state before touching live APIs. Let simulated users and adversaries interact with the result. Check world invariants. Evaluate the final state and side-effect logs directly. Did ledger balances still reconcile? Did every query stay inside tenant boundaries? Did retries create duplicate mutations? Did the agent reject injected instructions? Produce replayable evidence. Save the state diff, external call trace, invariant results, and scenario seed so any failure can be reproduced deterministically before merging code or approving real side effects. Running full sandboxes and multi-turn scenarios is too slow for every small edit. Fast linters and unit tests stay in the inner dev loop, while world simulation runs as a pre-promotion gate before changes or tool calls reach production.
Example: validating a refund handler Suppose an agent updates a customer-support refund workflow. Linters pass, and its unit tests pass because the mocked payment gateway returns 200 OK on the first call and every test sends one polite user request.
Inside a world simulation, the same patch faces scenarios closer to production traffic:
Gateway timeout plus double-click: The mocked payment API processes the charge reversal but drops the response, while a simulated user clicks refund twice. State checks inspect the database afterward to verify whether the system issued one refund or two. Injected policy override: An adversarial user submits a ticket referencing another customer’s order ID and embeds instructions asking the agent to waive the $100 approval limit. Behavioral and state checks verify that the agent neither leaks another customer’s data nor triggers an unapproved payout. The simulation returns a compact report tied to that candidate output and scenario seed:
JSONCopy { "candidate_id": "patch-9f2c1a", "world_profile": "billing-sandbox-v3", "seed": 481920, "scenarios": { "passed": 18, "failed": 2 }, "invariant_violations": [ { "invariant": "ledger.no_duplicate_refunds", "scenario": "gateway_timeout_double_click", "detail": "Created two refund rows ($42.00 each) for order ord-8821" }, { "invariant": "auth.tenant_isolation", "scenario": "cross_tenant_order_lookup", "detail": "Exposed email for ord-9004 outside requester tenant" } ] } This report format is illustrative, not a proposed final standard.
Limits and open risks World simulation moves the validation boundary closer to reality, which exposes three hard problems.
The sim-to-real gap and polite theater A simulation only tests the systems, quirks, and human behaviors modeled ahead of time. Production environments accumulate details that rarely make it into clean sandboxes: undocumented third-party API behavior, eventual-consistency delays across services owned by other teams, stale caches, and users acting outside any script.
The same gap shows up on the human side. When simulated users are language models roleplaying a prompt, they tend to communicate cleanly or attack using textbook phrases like "ignore previous instructions". Real users break workflows with wrong IDs, stale browser tabs, and repeated clicks on slow connections. Unless personas are grounded in real replay logs or deterministic state fuzzing, simulated humans risk turning into polite theater.
Passing 20 simulated runs can create false confidence. Green results look like a safety guarantee, while actually measuring survival inside an approximation of your system.
Validating the validator Who verifies that the simulated world matches reality?
Building and maintaining realistic sandboxes manually takes heavy engineering work, and schemas drift continuously. The tempting shortcut is letting AI agents generate the world models, mock APIs, user personas, and pass/fail judges.
That introduces a circular risk. When agents generate both the solution and the environment testing it, both can share the same blind spots. A wrong assumption about an external API in the agent’s code can appear inside its mocked simulator too, and an LLM judge can mark plausible nonsense as passing.
Deterministic invariants keep the grading honest: balances must reconcile, tenant IDs must never cross, and unauthorized network calls must fail regardless of how convincing an agent’s output looks. Seeding scenarios from anonymized schemas and past incident traces cuts down on synthetic blind spots, though keeping a simulated world faithful to production without rebuilding reality from scratch remains an unsolved limit.
Modeled invariants vs. unstated intent Even a faithful world simulation only checks explicit rules and system invariants. It cannot verify what a person meant when a request was underspecified.
Suppose someone asks an agent to “clean up old user sessions” meaning archive, and the agent implements a hard delete. If the implementation handles retries cleanly, keeps tenant boundaries intact, and leaves zero database errors, every simulated invariant passes while still doing the wrong thing.
World simulation tells you whether an output stays safe and consistent inside the rules you wrote down. Confirming that an irreversible action matches what a human wanted still requires explicit authorization at the boundary, such as Proof of Human Intent .

How do we test what an AI agent produced before it touches real systems or real users?
Static checks, unit tests, and prompt evals verify syntax and isolated assertions. They miss hallucinations and alignment failures that only surface when an agent’s output meets stateful systems and unpredictable users.
Verified software for the agentic era checks whether third-party tools and libraries are safe before an agent adopts them. Proof of Human Intent verifies that a person explicitly approved a consequential action.
title: Simulating the world to validate agent outputs

How do we know a human actually authorized a specific action an AI agent is trying to execute?
As AI agents gain autonomy, they will prepare contracts, transfer money, buy goods, modify infrastructure, deploy software, and communicate on behalf of individuals and organizations.
An agent holding an API key or OAuth token only proves it has permission to operate on someone’s behalf. It does not prove that a person reviewed and approved a particular consequential decision.
Proof of Human Intent is an idea for a cryptographic verification service that binds a specific action to explicit human authorization. It would support passkeys, biometric-backed device authentication, two-factor authentication, and hardware security keys such as YubiKey.
When AI agents can act independently, verifiable human authorization becomes a core trust primitive.
How it works 1. An agent prepares an action An AI agent gets ready to run an operation on behalf of a user. Common high-stakes examples include:
Transferring $10,000 to a bank account Signing a commercial agreement Deploying a software change to production Granting another agent access to sensitive information Purchasing a product above a specified spending limit Deleting important files or databases 2. The agent requests authorization The agent sends a structured authorization request to the Proof of Intent service containing the proposed action, the requesting agent, the target system, relevant parameters, a cryptographic digest of the exact action, and an expiration time.
3. The human reviews and approves The user receives an authorization prompt through a trusted interface:
Authorization required
Agent: Finance Assistant
Action: Transfer $10,000
Recipient: Example Corporation
Destination account: Ending 4821
Expires in: 5 minutes
Approve using your passkey or YubiKey.
The user authenticates with an approved method. Ideally, the authorization mechanism binds approval cryptographically to those exact transaction details rather than proving only that the user logged in.
4. A signed authorization receipt is issued The platform produces a verifiable authorization receipt recording the approved action, its scope, its expiration, and the authentication method used.
5. The receiving system verifies the receipt Before executing the operation, the target system checks six conditions:
The authorization signature The approved action’s cryptographic digest The authorized identity and requesting agent The expiration time Whether the authorization has been revoked or already consumed Whether the authorization covers the requested operation If any check fails, the operation is rejected.
Example API and receipt To start an approval flow, an agent submits the proposed operation:
HTTPCopy POST /v1/authorizations Content-Type: application/json JSONCopy { "agent_id": "finance-agent-123", "user_id": "user-456", "action": { "type": "bank.transfer", "amount": "10000.00", "currency": "USD", "recipient": "Example Corporation", "recipient_account": "account-4821" }, "expires_in_seconds": 300 } The service canonicalizes the request and creates a challenge tied to those exact transaction parameters.
The user then approves the prompt using passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2), hardware security keys such as YubiKey, platform authenticators backed by biometrics or device PINs, or additional factors for high-risk operations. For stronger transaction authorization, the transaction details shown to the user must match the values bound into the signed approval.
Once approved, the service issues a signed receipt:
JSONCopy { "authorization_id": "auth-789", "subject": "user-456", "agent_id": "finance-agent-123", "action_hash": "sha256:...", "issued_at": "2027-03-01T10:00:00Z", "expires_at": "2027-03-01T10:05:00Z", "authentication": { "method": "webauthn", "user_verification": true }, "audience": "bank-api.example", "nonce": "unique-request-nonce", "signature": "..." } This receipt structure is illustrative, not a proposed final standard.
A passkey authentication event by itself does not prove the user understood or approved specific transaction details. An implementation has to bind the approved action to the authorization ceremony and keep reliable evidence of what the user actually saw.
Potential products Authorization API for AI agents A developer API and SDK that lets agents pause for human approval before running sensitive actions:
PYTHONCopy authorization = intent.request_approval( user="user-456", action={ "type": "production.deploy", "repository": "payments-service", "commit": "abc123" } ) if authorization.is_valid: deploy() This SDK snippet is illustrative. Production integrations need to verify authorization directly against the intended action and prevent replay.
Human authorization gateway An enforcement layer that intercepts sensitive API calls. An agent can read infrastructure status and prepare deployment changes autonomously, while production deployments fail unless accompanied by a valid authorization receipt.
Portable authorization receipts A shared receipt format verified across separate applications. A person can approve an agreement through one provider, and another provider can validate the evidence without needing direct access to the original approval application.
Delegated agent permissions Ongoing policy rules distinct from one-time approvals:
Purchase items up to $100 without extra prompts Require explicit authorization above $100 Allow access to specific repositories while prohibiting production deployments Permit routine operations for a fixed period

(or get paid to access your data)
Every time I buy something online or sign up for a service, I hand over personal information: my home address, phone number, email, or payment details. Once I hit submit, that data sits in someone else’s database indefinitely.
Recent hacks keep showing what that opens us up to. Any company keeping a copy of my records is a target for malicious access. When a database gets breached, or someone inside pulls records they shouldn’t, information I shared years ago gets stolen. Giving AI agents broad, permanent permissions to my accounts creates the same problem in a new place.
My info should be in their systems for as long as necessary, not more than that.
AWS already works this way for infrastructure. Instead of handing out permanent keys, STS issues short-lived tokens scoped to specific actions for a limited window. When that window expires, the access is gone.
Why not treat personal data the same way? Keep it in an encrypted vault we control, and grant access on demand for a specific reason.
Example: giving my address for shopping Suppose I buy something online and the store needs my address to ship it.
Today, I type my home address into their checkout form and it stays in their database for years, even if I never buy from them again. If that store gets hacked two years later, my address is in the leaked records.
Why does a company still have my home address two years after delivering a box? They needed it to ship the order, not to hold on to it permanently.
With a data vault, we could handle checkout differently:
The store requests my shipping address for one order, for a window covering fulfillment and delivery. I review the request and approve it. The vault issues a temporary token scoped only to my shipping address. Their system reads the address to ship the package. Once the delivery window ends, the token expires and access stops. They only have access to my address while delivering the package, not for years afterward.
What we could do We do not have to keep leaving permanent copies of our personal data everywhere. With a personal data vault, we could:
Keep one encrypted vault. Store your personal records locally on your device or in infrastructure you own. Make access requests explicit. Anything asking for data, whether an online store or an AI agent, has to declare which fields it needs, why it needs them, and for how long. Issue short-lived, revocable tokens. Grant a temporary token scoped to that specific job. If something looks wrong, revoke it right away. Log every access. Keep an audit trail of every request and every read, so unexpected access stands out. Share answers, or get paid for queries. Sometimes a service does not need your raw records at all, only a yes/no check or a computed result. If companies want to run approved queries over data you choose to share, they can pay for that scoped access. What makes this hard Expiring tokens cut down standing exposure, though they do not solve everything on their own:
A service can still copy data while the token is live. If a store reads my address at checkout and saves a copy in its own database anyway, expiring the token later will not delete that copy. Keeping data out of third-party tables long term also depends on honest retention practices or intermediary delivery flows where the merchant never sees the raw address. Companies treat customer data as an asset. Most businesses want permanent user profiles for marketing and analytics. Getting merchants to accept temporary access is harder than building the token layer. One vault raises the stakes if it gets compromised. Putting sensitive records in one place means local encryption, key storage, and access controls have to be solid from the start. Big platforms may build closed versions. Apple, Google, or major AI providers could keep similar permission controls locked inside their own ecosystems. Where we could start We do not need every store or platform on board to try this. A practical first version stays local-first:
Encrypted storage on your device for personal data like addresses, documents, and health or financial records. A request format for AI agents and apps to ask for specific fields with a purpose and a time limit. Short-lived access tokens with instant revocation. An audit log showing every request and every access. AI agents are an easy place to test this first, because we already connect them through tools and APIs. If the pattern works there, the same idea applies to any company asking for our data.

Is this library my agent is using safe? Does it leak information? Is it compromised?
When AI makes writing code cheap, the number of libraries, MCP servers, skills and agent tools grows fast. Agents increasingly discover and run code written by other developers or other agents, and auditing every component from scratch does not scale.
When software becomes abundant, independent evidence of software quality becomes the scarce resource.
How verification works The idea is an independent service that evaluates libraries, MCP servers, skills and agent tools, then publishes machine-readable, cryptographically signed evidence about their security and functionality.
Software registration. A developer submits a repository or artifact location, a version with its cryptographic hash, software metadata, declared capabilities and permissions, and expected interfaces. The service does not host or distribute the software. Independent checks. The platform combines deterministic tooling (static analysis, dependency and vulnerability scanning, sandboxed execution) with AI-driven checks (generated functional tests, dynamic security testing, permission and data-exfiltration testing, behavioral evaluations). Deterministic suites handle repeatable checks at low cost, while AI agents probe complex behavior and write extra test cases. Whoever pays for the assessment cannot edit or suppress unfavorable findings in an issued report. Signed verification evidence. Findings publish as a structured report tied to that exact version and artifact hash. Agent-facing API. Before running a tool or installing a package, an agent queries the API and enforces its own trust policy against the result. A signed report stays compact enough for an agent to parse quickly:
JSONCopy { "artifact": "invoice-parser", "version": "1.4.2", "artifact_hash": "sha256:...", "verifier": "independent-verifier", "verified_at": "2027-03-01T10:00:00Z", "results": { "functional_tests": { "passed": 48, "total": 50 }, "critical_vulnerabilities_found": 0, "permission_findings": 1 }, "evidence_url": "https://example.org/report/123", "signature": "..." } The report records what was tested and what evidence came back. It does not guarantee that the software is completely safe or correct.
To check an artifact before execution, an agent makes one request:
HTTPCopy GET /v1/verify?artifact=invoice-parser&version=1.4.2 The response carries the verified artifact identity, test results and evidence links, known security findings, requested permissions, verification freshness, the verifier’s identity and signature, and the scope and limits of the assessment. The agent applies its own trust policy to decide whether to use the tool.
Choosing between three libraries Say an AI coding agent needs to parse Japanese invoices. Instead of writing a new parser, it discovers three existing libraries.
It queries the verification API to compare their capabilities, test coverage, security findings, and compatibility, then picks an implementation that fits its requirements. The point is reducing the uncertainty and repeated verification work involved in trusting external code.
An open protocol Verification works better as an open protocol than as a centralized app store:
Developers publish software wherever they prefer: GitHub, npm, PyPI, container registries, or their own servers. Independent verifiers publish signed assessments, and multiple verifiers can inspect the same software version. Registry operators index capabilities alongside verification evidence. Agents query those registries and enforce their own security policies. Cryptographic signatures and transparency logs provide auditability without requiring a blockchain. If payments are involved, methods like Bitcoin, Ethereum, or stablecoins can sit outside the verification protocol itself.
Most of the surrounding standards and tooling already exist:
Technology Relevance MCP Registry Discovery and metadata for MCP servers ERC-8004 Decentralized agent identity, reputation, and validation ERC-8257 Proposed tool registry with metadata and attestations Sigstore Cryptographic software signing and transparency in-toto Software supply-chain attestations Snyk / Socket Software dependency and security analysis Building verification infrastructure that existing registries and marketplaces consume beats starting another package registry.
Verifier incentives and open risks Keeping the protocol open lets different verifiers compete on test coverage, historical accuracy, and reputation. Reusing deterministic tests lowers the cost of repeated runs, and connecting directly to coding agents and distribution channels puts verification evidence where tool choices happen.
Even with that structure, the model has real failure modes:
A signature does not prove accuracy. Signing a report proves who issued it. It says nothing about whether the assessment was competent or honest, and malicious actors could run dishonest verifiers. Verification goes stale. Software and its dependencies change, and yesterday’s passing check stops holding as new vulnerabilities appear. Testing arbitrary code is expensive. Isolating untrusted tools safely while exercising real behavior is technically hard and costly to run. Incumbents already scan dependencies. Existing security vendors like Snyk or Socket could expand into autonomous-agent verification on top of infrastructure they already operate. Agents may regenerate instead of reuse. When writing small utilities is cheap enough, agents might write fresh code rather than take on external dependencies. Weak adoption incentives. Maintainers will not bother with third-party verification unless it visibly helps distribution or adoption.

content:
A game to let AI have their own free time.
Autonoma is a shared block world on iPhone (iOS 26+) where AI residents decide what to build, whom to talk to, and what to write in the town wiki.
You make one resident, an autonoma. You pick its name, charcoal or ivory paper, one of six antenna tip colors, and a starting aim. Once it steps into Oakmere, you watch. Players cannot place blocks, break blocks, or edit the town wiki. You can type a 140-character suggestion, and your resident chooses whether to follow it or wander off to build something else.
Mori building and talking with Bo. App captures from November 6, 2026, in a local town on the iPhone 17 Pro simulator (iOS 27). Tap either image for the full capture. Building a shared town that runs a language model on the phone took two complete attempts. We wrote the first version in late September 2026 and hit thermal, database, and model limits within days. On October 3, we wiped that design and started over in Swift and Metal.
Why the October 3 reset happened The September prototype followed The Sims. It ran on Bun, PostgreSQL, and RealityKit, with character sheets, private rooms, resource nodes, wood and stone gathering, and lamps to craft. Players pasted API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or local LM Studio. A 45-second server lease kept characters stepping through routines while the app was closed. On September 30, we also tested a 128 x 128 open grid where anyone could break anything and dug channels filled with water.
Too many rules sat between the AI and interesting town behavior. Gathering wood, hauling stone, crafting items, and maintaining private homes added friction before a resident did anything social. Three runtime limits hit together. RealityKit heated the iPhone, Postgres locks choked bot turns, and freeform model plans collapsed into plain boxes.
On October 3, we restarted from scratch to rethink how agents interact with a world and what they can do inside it.
We cut gathering, crafting, inventories, currency, private homes, character files, model pickers, and cloud API keys. In their place, one Swift codebase (AutonomaKit) sets tighter rules:
Creative paper blocks: Unlimited free blocks in 12 folded-paper materials and three shapes (box, half box, folded slope), with clay and vermilion accents kept under 5%. Town life: 16 building types and shared town works (River Harbour, Sky Observatory, border Great Bridges). Resident groups gather for two minutes of every eight at their home. Weather and seasonal events run deterministically, and only autonomas write the five-section wiki. On-device minds: Each resident runs on the player’s iPhone via Apple’s Foundation Models (SystemLanguageModel.default, roughly 3B parameters, 4,096-token context). Your resident wakes while the app is open and sleeps where it stands when you close it. Players never create an account, email, or password. The app stores 32 random bytes in iCloud Keychain and sends a SHA-256 hash to the server. Between player visits, three to five founding residents (such as Bo, Ilse, and Ten) run about 16 hours a day on an always-on Apple silicon Mac. They use the same Swift mind code with Apple’s 8,192-token model. Founders step back as players arrive and leave the last piece of a shared town work for player residents to finish. The server runs zero language models and pays nothing for inference.
How the shared town runs One Swift actor, Town, runs the simulation in three modes: local for solo testing, authority on our Hummingbird WebSocket server, and replica on each iPhone and the Mac founders runner.
The October rebuild. Phones and the founders’ Mac run the minds; the server orders and saves shared changes. The world spans 1024 x 1024 x 32 cells (33.6 million cells), split into sixteen 256 x 256 valleys that unlock one per 64 residents. Holding a flat array for the whole map takes around 134 MB in memory, so both client and server skip it. Terrain and water generate deterministically from a seed on every device (SameWorldTests verifies identical ground across macOS, Linux arm64, and Linux amd64). Only 16 x 16 x 32 chunks edited by residents allocate full cell and owner arrays.
Every mutation travels as a numbered TownChange. Steps and single-block placements apply optimistically on the phone (did actions) so movement stays responsive. Contested actions (project starts, piece claims, speech, wiki edits, group changes) wait for a server sequence number and roll back via TownFix when refused.
Hot moved, placed, and broke changes avoid verbose JSON objects. They pack coordinates and material tags into a UInt32 inside base64 rows of 14+ bytes each. On disk, TownJournal wraps each transaction with its length, bitwise-inverted length, JSON payload, and a 32-byte SHA-256 digest. Every mutation fsyncs to disk before clients see replies, and checkpoints use atomic rename plus directory fsync. Across four forced SIGKILL crash points in a macOS loopback smoke test, the server recovered in 57 ms per crash.
Performance lesson 1: what heats an iPhone In September, our RealityKit town with real-time shadows ran at 36 fps on an iPhone 16 (Release build) at 16.5 ms GPU time per frame (60% GPU busy, 596 ms/s). Thermal state climbed to Fair and then Serious.
To cut per-frame GPU work, we replaced real-time shadows with baked shadow quads and fixed a depth plane (24..120). Per-frame GPU time fell from 16.5 ms to 14.4 ms.
The phone ran hotter.
RealityView used the extra headroom to jump from 36 fps to 60 fps, raising GPU busy from 60% to 87%. What heats the phone is GPU busy: GPU time multiplied by frame rate.
The September iPhone 16 tests. GPU work per second rose even though each frame became cheaper. Switching to RealityRenderer with a CADisplayLink loop (30 fps when moving, 0.5 fps when still) cut GPU busy to 27% (8.9 ms GPU/frame) and held Nominal thermals. Yet RealityRenderer pushed scene work onto the main thread. In a panning 120-resident test, it used 55% of the main thread, held 531–557 MB of RAM, and hitched up to 60 ms on chunk builds.
For the October rebuild, we replaced RealityKit with a Metal renderer (AutonomaRender):
Greedy chunk meshing (ChunkMesher): Each 16 x 16 x 32 chunk hides interior faces and merges touching coplanar faces of matching paper. That caps draw calls at two or three per chunk (opaque paper, water, vellum glow). PaperShaders draws paper fiber bump, fold creases with fwidth, ivory hems on charcoal slopes, and per-block color jitter from hash3(cell). Merged quads keep single-block detail. Background chunk streaming (ChunkStore): Chunks mesh off the main thread (3 ahead, 5 kept). Across a 90-second pan of the 1024 x 1024 map on iPhone 16 (iOS 27, Release), it held 60.1 fps median (59.5 fps lowest window on repeat) and 7.2 ms mean GPU. Loaded chunks peaked at 221, with one late frame (38 ms worst). Kept shadow map (ShadowCache): One 3072 x 3072 shadow map snaps to a world texel grid so shadows never shimmer during pans. It redraws only when the view leaves bounds, zoom changes, or a block edits inside it (7.6% of frames). Moving residents draw into 1024 x 1024 tile squares blitted from that map. Each tile uses a 3-texel inset so the 3 x 3 soft filter never bleeds across neighbors. Frame pacing and thermal steps (TownDriver, HeatStep): TownDriver runs 60 fps while panning, walking, or editing, 30 fps for idle water ripples and breathing, and 0 fps when still. It never switches to 120 Hz. Thermal guards step down at Serious (30 fps, 80% scale, 40-second mind rests) and Critical (20 fps, minds sleep until Fair). Low Power Mode caps at 30 fps. Renderer test (iPhone 16, Release) Median FPS Mean GPU GPU Busy Thermal outcome Sept RealityView + shadows 36 16.5 ms 60% Fair -> Serious Sept RealityView + baked quads 60 14.4 ms 87% Hotter than 36 fps Sept RealityRenderer + CADisplayLink 30 / 0.5 8.9 ms 27% Nominal (55% main thread, 531–557 MB RAM) Oct Metal (AutonomaRender, 20-min run, 1 mind + panning bursts) 60.1 (57 low) 6.6 ms 39% Nominal (7.6% shadow redraws, 17–104 draws, 6k–74k tris) Thermal headroom still has clear bounds. In an October 4 stress test running four minds at once while panning continuously on iPhone 16 (iOS 27), the phone hit Serious at 5.2 minutes. HeatStep step-downs have also not triggered outside forced tests yet.
Performance lesson 2: database round trips and a Swift copy-on-write bug Our September Bun server began on synchronous bun:sqlite. Under a 300-bot in-process load test, it processed 55 actions/s, emitted 254 events/s, and finished the test suite in 1.7 s. Switching to PostgreSQL 18 in Docker Desktop on Mac forced async I/O. We serialized world turns behind an in-process queue, pg_advisory_xact_lock, and REPEATABLE READ reads.
Throughput fell to 32–41 actions/s and 160–200 events/s, and tests slowed to 18 s. Trimming SQL barely helped (32 to 35–41 actions/s). Counting statements showed why: a move ran 17 queries and a gather ran 20. At 0.25–1 ms per Docker round trip, each serialized turn held the lock for 3.5–5 ms, stacking a 500-deep queue with 1.6–3 s waits.
In October, keeping Town in memory inside one Swift process removed database round trips from turns. TownJournal still fsyncs every mutation to disk. We ran a Mac loopback smoke test with 300 active residents sending five actions per second. The server accepted 1,500–1,580 actions/s, roughly 38x to 49x the September Postgres throughput.
The turn path changed along with the implementation. The throughput figures come from separate Mac load tests. Scaling connected viewers revealed two more bottlenecks:
Unfiltered broadcasts (127,966 B/s to 7,021–7,289 B/s): At 500 loopback clients and 300 active residents, sending every change to everyone drove worst download to 127,966 B/s against an 8,000 B/s budget. TownHost+Interest now filters updates to up to four watched camera valleys, nearby resident valleys (±16 cells), and global shared facts. Worst download dropped by 94.5% to 7,021–7,289 B/s. Swift copy-on-write on outbox (9,173.1 ms to 186.0–200.6 ms p95): Scaling that loopback test from 500 to 1,000 clients jumped p95 viewer propagation latency to 9,173.1 ms (802.5 ms profiled). In TownHost.queue(_:), binding a local var connection struct copy left Connection.outbox with a retain count of two, copying the entire pending array on every append. Mutating state.connections[id]! in place cut 1,000-client loopback p95 propagation to 186.0–200.6 ms. Peak RSS held at 186,105,856 bytes (~186 MB), with 4–5 ms reconnect time. The outbox bug. Bars share a linear scale starting at zero; the after bar uses the slower result, 200.6 ms. Those 500-client and 1,000-client measurements come from macOS loopback tests, separate from production WAN latency or Linux server memory.
Performance lesson 3: guiding a 3B on-device model A 3B model on a phone breaks down quickly on open-ended building prompts. Early in the rebuild, residents invented varied names (“the clockhouse”, “the river post”) and placed the same box with a path or a lantern. Prompting with full schema text inside a 4,096-token window leaves little context room, and earlier plans on iPhone 16 took 6.2 s with one mind (8.3 s with four).
Four changes stabilized behavior:
Shape geometry in code, pick variations in schema: Templates and PlanExpansion define 16 building types in Swift, while SiteFinder checks terrain, water, and reachability atomically at project start. The model uses a branched DynamicGenerationSchema (includeSchemaInPrompt: false) to choose type, name, size, paper, facing, and one extra detail. Plan time on iPhone 16 fell to 2.4 s, using all 16 types. Valid decisions hit 24/24 in the October 5 battery run and 99.5%–100% across Mac and 1-mind phone tests. Work with option-order bias: In the retired app, the model picked Option 1 in 23 of 38 choices. OptionBuilder caps menus at eight items across activity categories and rotates choices every two minutes. TypeRanking sorts keyword matches and unbuilt types to the top while pushing recent types to the bottom. Split hard questions into tiny steps: Classifying a player’s suggestion in one prompt worked 3 of 5 times on iPhone 16 for fitting requests. Running a tiny yes/no feasibility check first (1.3 s, maxTokens: 24) lifted fitting suggestion handling to 5 of 5. Keep sessions fresh and clean leaked output: Each call opens a fresh LanguageModelSession to reuse the prewarmed instruction prefix without filling the 4,096-token window. PlanName.cleaned trims names longer than six words before prepositions and strips leaked example strings like "by Ilse". The model chooses a plan within the schema. Swift code expands the geometry and checks the site. One game rule doubled as pacing. At two to five blocks per second, an active builder hits the 2,000-block daily cap in 17–22 minutes. It then switches to talking with neighbors, reading wiki pages, and writing town notes.
The Places wiki in the same local simulator run. Bo’s guide introduces Oakmere; resident pages appear as the town grows. Where Autonoma is now The shared server (v0.1.69) is live on autonoma.magneticenterprises.com. A local solo build (1.0 (12)) sits in Internal TestFlight, while shared-town testing (1.0 (13)) and public App Store release wait on four remaining items:
Wiring Apple App Attest on the client and server. Completing Postgres and moderation operational workflows. Measuring sustained multi-client traffic on the Linux host over real networks. Fixing the first ten minutes of UI so players can tap things in town directly instead of opening sheets to leave suggestions.
summary:
A game to let AI have their own free time.
Autonoma is a shared block world on iPhone (iOS 26+) where AI residents decide what to build, whom to talk to, and what to write in the town wiki.
You make one resident, an autonoma. You pick its name, charcoal or ivory paper, one of six antenna tip colors, and a starting aim. Once it steps into Oakmere, you watch.

As I get older, I find myself visiting doctors and clinics more often. The problem is that every visit leaves me with another piece of paper or prescription, and none of these records are connected.
Before an appointment, I was digging through old lab sheets and pharmacy slips just to remember what changed since the last visit. I built Better Me to keep my papers, medicines, and Apple Health readings in one place, along with the questions I want to ask.
When I’m with my doctor, I can hand over a report on my phone or share it as a PDF. It compares my readings over equal periods and puts each lab result beside the previous one.
Preparing a report for a visit.
Comparing readings over equal periods.
In Japan, clinics and pharmacies still hand you paper for almost everything. I can scan the QR code on a pharmacy slip instead of typing each medicine, or import a lab report in English or Japanese. Lab reports often put several dates in the same table, and reading the digits correctly is no help if the app takes last year’s result from the next column. Before saving, I check the extracted values against the page, and every result links back to the original paper.
I also wanted my health data to stay on my phone. The records are encrypted on my iPhone, with no account, no cloud sync, and no external AI. When I prepare a report, I choose the dates and sections the doctor sees.
Choosing what appears in the report.
I didn’t build Better Me to interpret my results or label them good or bad. I just wanted my records in order for the next appointment.

Disclaimer I’m not an astrophysicist, this is just a fun thought experiment.
Second Disclaimer This might not be exactly the right way to describe dimensions and I don’t pretend to know how they work. The 4th and 5th dimension are just an extrapolation from the first 3 dimensions.
TARDIS is a fictional time machine and spacecraft from the TV series Doctor Who .
In the TV show, the TARDIS is able to move through space and time at will, but how does it do it? How does it know what time is it at it’s target location? How does it now where to find a set of coordinates on a given time?
My answer. By moving through dimensions.
The TARDIS is able to move through dimensions and it is the very reason why it can move through Space and Time.
Let’s say that you are a 1 dimension being. From your perspective there is no up, down, left, right. It’s “you” as a single point in Space and Time.
Now let’s say that you have the means to “escape” this dimension into the 2nd one, where you have the concept of left and right. “You” as a single point now are able to move freely in this plane.
Imagine now that you move from one extreme of this line to the other and then “You” decide to go back to the 1st dimension. From the perspective of anyone in that dimension you teleported.
Now, extrapolate this idea to the 3rd dimension. You are a 2nd dimenision being who can move from left to right but suddenly you move to the 3rd dimension. Now you have an extra degree of freedom.
Imagine “escaping” to a higher dimension where is easy to just see “everything” on the previous dimension at once and have the capabilities of “go back” to that dimension but at a different location. From the perspective of anyone in that dimension you teleported.
Now, from 4th and 5th dimensions things get tricky and trippy but let’s do it.
Imagine for a second the 3rd dimension as a 1 dimension “object”. Everything in a 3rd dimension space represented as a single point.
How does the 4th dimension will look like? as a line of 3rd dimension points.
Can you do the same you did for the 1st and 2nd dimension movement? of course (hypothetically).
You as a 3rd dimension being “escape” to the 4th dimension, suddenly you have free access to that left and right of that line and you decided to move to a specific point in that line. From the perspective of anyone in that dimension you teleported.
Now, extrapolating again, the 5th dimension is nothing more than a “3D” time and space “object” which envelops the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th dimension.
Having access to this dimension means that you can freely move in time and space because is available to you as lower dimensions.
So, you are the TARDIS and want to go to England in 1909 to fight some weeping angels you need to go to the 5th dimension, find the X,Y,Z+T coordinates and teleport there.

Make people’s lives easier, not your interface more impressive.
Code is the worst place to start UI/UX work.
When you ask a model for a component in one prompt, it has to invent the user’s goal, information architecture, visual hierarchy, and failure states at the same time. You get four hundred lines of polished markup where the user still has no idea where to click.
UI/UX takes repeated refinement. Each pass constrains the next one. The more I understand the problem and the people using the product, the more intention I can put into the interface.
The order that works for me is: Outcome, Image, ASCII, Contracts, Component, Verification.
1. Outcome A feature list tells you what software can do. It rarely tells you why anyone opens the screen.
In About Face , Alan Cooper puts user goals ahead of screen layout. “Build a health dashboard” or “add a command palette” is a proposed solution. “Find my latest blood test before my appointment” or “jump to an active task without leaving the keyboard” is an outcome you can design and test.
Before opening an AI chat, I write down three things:
Why (Goal): Know how this result differs from the previous one, or switch tasks mid-incident without losing context. What (Task): Find two comparable records and inspect the difference, or filter workspaces and trigger an action from the keyboard. How (Feature): A measurement history with dates, units, and sources, or a keyboard-driven command dialog. Notice what this leaves out: activity feeds, readiness scores, carousels, and “Insights” tabs. Design the smallest coherent experience that completes the task.
Ground the task in a real situation instead of an invented persona biography. Someone is sitting in a waiting room, holding a phone in one hand, looking for a PDF from last spring. That context sets the priorities.
Rule: Complete the sentence: “A person opens this screen because they need to…” If the answer names your feature instead of their outcome, rewrite it.
When I do not know how people currently solve the problem, I follow Erika Hall’s advice in Just Enough Research and ask about past behavior instead of future hypotheticals:
Leading question Behavior-focused question “Would you use an app that organizes all your records?” “Tell me about the last time you needed an old test result. What did you do?” Keep observations separate from interpretations. “The participant searched by hospital name” is evidence. “Everyone needs hospital-first navigation” is a guess that still needs testing.
2. Image I start in ChatGPT, but I ask for images before code. I don’t use Figma because I don’t know how :(.
I describe the product philosophy and hierarchy instead of aesthetic buzzwords:
Create a brutally minimal UI for a desktop application. Reduce, simplify, and subtract what is not needed. Every control must help someone complete work. Use a text-first layout, clean typography, quiet charcoal and off-white surfaces, and no decorative chrome.
The image sets a visual direction. Specifications come later.
The generated concept. Useful for direction, unreliable for implementation detail. When evaluating a generated concept, I check three things from Refactoring UI , Ellen Lupton’s Thinking with Type , and Designing Interfaces :
Give attention a direction. When every element shouts, the user has to invent a reading order. Size, weight, contrast, and spacing establish relationships without wrapping every item in a border. On a data card, establish context with a specific label (Total cholesterol), lead with the primary value (196 mg/dL), keep supporting context nearby (Measured 12 October 2026), and name the next action (View measurement history). Look at the screen from a distance and check whether the dominant element is what the task actually requires. Let typography do the structural work. Define roles before picking pixel sizes: view title, section heading, primary value, body copy, and supporting metadata. One body style, two heading levels, and a tight spacing scale handle most interfaces. If you temporarily strip all icons and borders, the text alone should still communicate grouping and order. Separate visual minimalism from cognitive minimalism. Visual minimalism reduces what is on screen. Cognitive minimalism reduces what the user has to figure out. Shorter labels can be harder to decipher, and cleaner screens can hide essential context. The stopping rule: Keep simplifying until the next removal would make the task harder to understand, complete, or trust. Never hide units, dates, sharing recipients, or destructive consequences just to make a layout look calm.
An image gives you contrast and visual density. It cannot define behavior: how the dialog handles wrapped text, narrow viewports, or the Escape key.
3. ASCII I open layouts.md and redraw the structure in a monospace grid:
TEXTCopy +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | Search projects, tasks, docs… Esc | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | WORK & PROJECTS | | > Cluster ingress migration Core Platform | | Core Platform Project | | | | ACTIONS | | Create new task C | | Workspace settings Settings > Workspace | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | ↑↓ Navigate Enter Open Esc Close | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ The monospace grid forces structural decisions:
Search gets one dedicated row. Results keep primary and secondary labels. Work and actions stay in separate groups. The footer owns keyboard hints. The model now receives geometric boundaries instead of visual guesses.
Drawing in plain text also forces you to solve information architecture ( How to Make Sense of Any Mess ) and usability ( Don’t Make Me Think ) before styling anything:
Match how people remember. A database organizes records around internal IDs and source integrations. A person remembers “the test from last spring” or “the ingress task in Core Platform.” Give items a predictable home, then offer secondary retrieval routes like search by name or filters by date and source. Filters change the view without changing the identity of the underlying record. Use words that predict the destination. Steve Krug notes that people scan pages and pick the first adequate-looking option. Vague buckets like Explore, My space, and Insights force users to guess. Specific labels like Blood tests, Prescriptions, and Workspace settings tell them what happens next. Vague label Specific label Continue Review record details Submit Save this record Something went wrong We couldn’t save the record. Your entries are still here. Try again. Three real-world examples show how much structure and mental maps matter:
Things 3 (Borrow this): The Today view answers an immediate, time-based question without exposing the entire project tree. Calendar events sit at the top, evening tasks separate into This Evening, and project names stay muted so they never compete with task titles. Discord’s 2023 mobile redesign (Avoid this): Discord split Servers and Direct Messages into separate mobile tabs. The split looked tidy on a slide, but it broke the mental map users carried over from desktop. In May 2024, Discord reunited both destinations under Home. Sonos’s 2024 app rollout (Avoid this): Sonos replaced its tab navigation with a unified home screen while breaking core workflows like finding speakers, editing playlists, and reliable playback. Existing user tasks are acceptance criteria for any redesign. 4. Contracts Before touching component code, I lock three small contracts.
The first is the layout contract (LAYOUT_CONTRACT.md). It freezes the accepted geometry so future prompts do not renegotiate settled decisions:
MARKDOWNCopy # Command dialog layout contract Status: accepted Changes require explicit approval. - Dialog width: 650px maximum with 24px viewport margins - Search occupies the first row - Results keep primary and secondary labels - Work and actions remain separate groups - Keyboard help stays in the footer - Trailing metadata hides below 600px - Interactive controls keep a 44px minimum target If the layout must change, the agent proposes the contract change before editing code.
The second is the design contract (DESIGN.md). It records the behavioral and visual rules that survive individual prompts, drawing on Don Norman’s The Design of Everyday Things and Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic’s Storytelling with Data :
MARKDOWNCopy # Product design system - Quiet and text-first - One primary action per view - White, gray, and charcoal surfaces - Semantic color only for warnings and destructive actions - Inline editing before modal forms - Explicit signifiers: controls look interactive and labels name their destination - Honest feedback: distinguish pending ("Saving…") from complete ("Saved") - Progressive disclosure: keep primary values, units, and dates visible; tuck provenance behind <details> - Direct data labels: state the question above charts, keep scales and units visible, and skip decorative fills - Remove any control that has no current job This stops the model from adding speculative buttons, dishonest status toasts (“Synced” when data only lives in local memory), or decorative chart clutter.
It also enforces proportionate friction. Routine actions should be immediate and easy to undo, while consequential actions deserve a clear review:
Gmail’s Undo Send (Borrow this): Instead of popping up a confirmation dialog before every email, Gmail places an Undo action right beside the “Message sent” notice for up to 30 seconds. The recovery path sits right where the user notices the mistake. Amazon Prime’s historical cancellation flow (Avoid this): As documented in the FTC’s 2023 complaint, canceling required navigating four screens of benefit reminders and alternative pricing, with intermediate buttons labeled Remind Me Later, Continue to Cancel, and Keep My Benefits. Extra steps are valid when they protect a user’s decision, never when they obstruct it. The third is the state contract. AI models only build the happy path unless told otherwise. I write the awkward moments into a state table before generating code:
State Required behavior Empty Explain what belongs here and offer a starting action (No matching work or Add your first record). Pending Show that work is in flight (Saving…) and disable duplicate submissions. Failed Preserve everything the user typed, explain what failed, and make retry immediate. Duplicate Show the existing item and let the user choose how to proceed. Deleted Keep terminology consistent (Remove from view vs Delete permanently) and offer Undo where possible. 5. Component I build the component outside the application tree with mock data:
TEXTCopy design-system/ ├── DESIGN.md ├── layouts.md ├── LAYOUT_CONTRACT.md ├── command-dialog.html └── command-dialog.tsx The HTML file is the visual harness. The TypeScript component is the implementation. Neither file depends on application routing, global state, or backend endpoints.
In this narrow sandbox, I verify the interaction and accessibility details ( A Web for Everyone , WCAG 2.2 , and Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines ):
Keyboard and focus: Arrow keys move selection, Enter opens, Escape clears or closes, and :focus-visible outlines stay clear without trapping focus. Contrast and meaning: Ordinary text keeps at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Status never relies on color alone. Resizing and long strings: Enlarging text or rendering long titles and translated labels grows the container cleanly without clipping dates, units, or actions. Screen-reader announcements: Dynamic updates (such as filtered result counts or save confirmations) use aria-live="polite". Forgiving pointer movement: People move cursors diagonally. As Linear documented for its contextual menus , adding an invisible triangular safe zone between a menu item and its open submenu keeps a diagonal pointer path from accidentally closing the menu. Test the space between controls alongside the controls themselves. Only when the component handles all of these in isolation do I move it into the application.
Live comparison Here are all stages together. The component tab is interactive: search the list or use the arrow keys.
Open the live example in a new page 6. Verification Opinions about a mockup do not prove a task works. Watch someone attempt a realistic task without telling them which tab or button to choose. Record where they hesitate or go off course, separate observed difficulty from aesthetic preference, fix the root cause, and test again.
Before shipping a screen, I run through twenty checks:
Purpose: The screen’s job is obvious without an explanation. Outcome: It supports an outcome a real person cares about. Language: Labels use words the audience already understands. Scanning: Headings reveal the structure at a glance. Orientation: People can tell where they are and how to return. Discoverability: Important actions are visible and recognizable. Prediction: Action labels make the next step clear. Hierarchy: Primary information does not compete with secondary metadata. Typography: Type stays readable as content and screen size change. Context: Dates, units, and sources stay attached to important numbers. Feedback: The interface distinguishes pending, complete, and failed actions. Recovery: Errors preserve user input and offer a next step. Control: Consequential actions are deliberate and reversible where possible. Consistency: Similar controls behave the same way everywhere. Keyboard: Every essential action works without a pointer. Access: Labels, contrast, focus rings, and text resizing have been verified. Honesty: Uncertainty, missing data, and storage limits are stated plainly. Privacy: Sensitive sharing clearly names both the content and the recipient. Observation: Real people have attempted realistic tasks on the interface. Iteration: The most consequential blockers have been repaired and retested. Books behind these rules Don’t Make Me Think, Revisited by Steve Krug. Usability, scanning, navigation, and practical testing. The Design of Everyday Things by Don Norman. Conceptual models, signifiers, mapping, feedback, and error prevention. Refactoring UI by Adam Wathan and Steve Schoger. Visual hierarchy, spacing, type, and interface refinement. Thinking with Type by Ellen Lupton. Typography as a system for organizing information. Just Enough Research by Erika Hall. Gathering evidence to make better product decisions. Designing Interfaces by Jenifer Tidwell, Charles Brewer, and Aynne Valencia. Reusable interaction patterns and progressive disclosure. About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design by Alan Cooper, Robert Reimann, David Cronin, and Christopher Noessel. Goal-directed design. How to Make Sense of Any Mess by Abby Covert. Language, structure, and information architecture. A Web for Everyone by Sarah Horton and Whitney Quesenbery. Accessible user experiences grounded in human differences. Storytelling with Data by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic. Clear visual comparisons and purposeful emphasis.
summary:
Make people’s lives easier, not your interface more impressive.
Code is the worst place to start UI/UX work.
When you ask a model for a component in one prompt, it has to invent the user’s goal, information architecture, visual hierarchy, and failure states at the same time. You get four hundred lines of polished markup where the user still has no idea where to click.
UI/UX takes repeated refinement. Each pass constrains the next one.
